query: For a FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy alloy used as a thin coating on a conventional metal substrate, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs overall wear resistance and microscopic deformation during sliding in the intended high-temperature operating regime? Define a controlled change relative to a baseline coating condition, predict the corresponding directional changes in wear and deformation, state the regime in which those predictions should hold, identify supporting prior evidence, and specify a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Mild post‐deposition annealing of FeNiCrCoCu high‐entropy alloy coatings promotes surface segregation and in situ oxidation of Cu, leading to the formation of a continuous nanocrystalline Cu oxide layer that acts as a protective barrier during high-temperature sliding. This oxide layer reduces local stress concentrations and shifts the deformation mechanism from dislocation-dominated plasticity to grain-boundary sliding, thereby lowering wear rates compared to the as-deposited condition.
generation.material_initial_state: As-deposited FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy alloy thin coating on a conventional metal substrate (without any thermal treatment)
generation.intervention: Perform a controlled mild annealing treatment (e.g., at ~300 °C for a fixed time) to induce Cu surface segregation and oxidation
generation.conditions: High-temperature sliding wear regime (e.g., sliding tests conducted at ~300 °C under similar loads to the intended operating conditions)
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of a continuous, adherent nanocrystalline Cu oxide (e.g., CuO) layer at the coating surface and along grain boundaries
generation.mechanism: Post-deposition annealing induces Cu segregation; under high-temperature sliding, localized tribochemical oxidation converts segregated Cu into a protective oxide layer that reduces friction and alters the deformation mechanism from intra-granular dislocation glide to grain-boundary-mediated processes
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the as-deposited baseline, the annealed coating will exhibit a lower wear rate, reduced coefficient of friction, and microscopic evidence of diminished plastic deformation (e.g., fewer dislocation features and more grain-boundary sliding signatures) during high-temperature sliding
generation.boundary: Predictions are expected to hold under high-temperature sliding conditions (around 300 °C) where tribochemical reactions are active; behavior under significantly higher temperatures may involve additional mechanisms
generation.uncertainty: The exact kinetics of Cu segregation and oxide formation, the critical annealing parameters needed to achieve an optimal oxide layer, and the durability of the protective layer under prolonged sliding and cyclic thermal loading remain to be fully quantified

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy alloy coated substrates. Subject one set to a mild annealing treatment (e.g., 300 °C for 1 hour) and keep the other set as-deposited. Conduct sliding wear tests at 300 °C under identical load and speed conditions. Use surface microscopy (SEM/TEM) and microstructural analysis (EDX, XRD) to characterize the presence and continuity of the Cu oxide layer, and measure wear rates and friction coefficients for both sets.
measurements: Surface and cross-sectional microstructure via SEM/TEM
Phase identification via XRD/EDS to confirm Cu oxide formation
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the annealed coatings do not show a statistically significant reduction in wear rate or friction coefficient, nor display the continuous nanocrystalline Cu oxide layer and a shift in deformation mechanism when compared to the as-deposited coatings under high-temperature sliding, then the hypothesis is falsified.

Question: How can a nanocrystalline refractory high-entropy alloy (RHEA) film with superior mechanical and tribological properties be synthesized using a cost-effective single target, and what are the effects of annealing on its adhesion and wear performance?. System: Equimolar CuMoTaWV refractory high-entropy alloy (RHEA) film deposited on silicon and 304 stainless-steel substrates. Processing: DC-magnetron sputtering using a single target prepared by partial spark plasma sintering (SPS) of equimolar elemental powders (Cu, Mo, Ta, W, V) at 1000 °C under 40 MPa pressure; film deposition at 500 °C substrate temperature for 120 min in Ar atmosphere (1.16 × 10⁻³ mPa, 150 W power); post-deposition annealing at 300 °C for adhesion improvement. Test conditions: Nanoindentation at 3 mN load; nanopillar compression (440 nm diameter, 3 mN max force); tribological wear tests at room temperature (RT) and 300 °C with 1 N load and 0.1 m/s sliding speed against E52100 alloy steel counterballs. Findings: The as-deposited film exhibited a nanocrystalline body-centered cubic (BCC) solid solution with an average grain size of 18 nm and a thickness of ~900 nm.; Nanoindentation measurement

Question: How does the wear behaviour of a powder metallurgically produced AlCoCrFeNiTi 0.5 high-entropy alloy change under reciprocating wear conditions at elevated temperatures, and what are the underlying mechanisms?. System: AlCoCrFeNiTi 0.5 high-entropy alloy (HEA). Processing: Inert gas atomisation using argon followed by spark plasma sintering (SPS) at 1050 °C for 10 min under 50 MPa compaction pressure, with passive cooling at 150 K/min until 300 °C.
